passage: On the school-bus stop in a Kolkata lane, five-year-old Binita spotted Divyansh across the road with his red ball. Her eyebrows jumped up and down once, quick as a blink, and she tilted her head toward the pavement, where two chalk squares were drawn. Divyansh didn't notice. She waited, then called, "Divyansh! Hopscotch?" and this time he crossed the road, grinning.

qa.q: What did Binita do with her eyebrows when she saw Divyansh?
qa.a: Her eyebrows jumped up and down once, quick as a blink.

qa.q: What does Binita's tilt of the head toward the chalk squares suggest she wants and feels?
qa.a: She seems eager and hopeful that Divyansh will see her hello and come over to play hopscotch. He may simply not have been looking, since he didn't notice.

qa.q: What made the invitation work in the end?
qa.a: She added a spoken invitation, "Divyansh! Hopscotch?", because the quick eyebrow flash was easy to miss.

qa.q: Why might Divyansh have missed the first signal?
qa.a: He may have been looking at his red ball or the traffic, and a signal that quick is easy to miss from across the road.

grounding: A quick eyebrow flash is a friendly signal that is easy to miss, so speaking adds clarity.

passage:
"Omkar, look at Dev over there," said Hemant, walking his son up the ramp of the community centre in Toronto.
"He did the face," said Omkar.
"What face?"
"The eyebrow face. It means come play."
Hemant looked. Dev's eyebrows flicked up once, and then Dev held up a toy digger.
"Should we say hello?"
"Hi, Dev!" shouted Omkar, already running.

qa.q: What did Omkar call the face that Dev made?
qa.a: He called it "the eyebrow face".

qa.q: What does Omkar think Dev's eyebrow flick means, and how does he feel about it?
qa.a: He thinks it means "come play" and is clearly excited, since he shouts "Hi, Dev!" and runs over at once. Dev could also have been greeting Hemant rather than inviting Omkar.

qa.q: What could Omkar add to make his answer clearer to Dev?
qa.a: He did it by shouting "Hi, Dev!", because a spoken greeting makes the signal clear to a child who might miss a quick eyebrow flick.

qa.q: What would Hemant notice if he hadn't asked about the face?
qa.a: He might have walked past without noticing, because the flick was quick and only Omkar seemed to catch it.

grounding: An eyebrow flash invites play, and a spoken hello makes the invitation clear.

passage:
Observation note, Anganwadi centre, written by Kashish (worker).
Today Madhuri, five, stood near the new girl at the sand tray and gave two quick eyebrow flashes, then held up a spoon. The new girl did not look up. Madhuri tried again, brows up and down, and then her smile faded and she stepped back. I knelt and said, “Your eyebrows were saying hello. Try saying it too.” Madhuri whispered, “Hello, want to dig?” The new girl nodded, and they filled the pail together for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Madhuri hold up after her eyebrow flashes?
qa.a: She held up a spoon.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri's smile fade after her second try?
qa.a: She probably felt disappointed and a little rejected because her friendly signal got no answer. She may also have felt unsure whether the new girl wanted to play at all.

qa.q: What worked when the eyebrow flash was missed?
qa.a: Kashish named what the eyebrows meant and suggested adding words, and saying “Hello, want to dig?” made the invitation clear.

qa.q: How might the new girl have experienced Madhuri's first attempts?
qa.a: She was busy looking at the sand, so she likely never saw the quick flashes and had no idea she was being invited.

grounding: The note shows a child using a quick eyebrow flash to invite play, the signal being missed, and a spoken greeting making it clear.

passage: The morning bus to the market stopped outside Sunaina's house, and Himani pressed her face to the window. Sunaina was on her doorstep with a skipping rope. Himani lifted both eyebrows high and dropped them, grinning. Sunaina just kept skipping. Himani did it again, bigger, until her forehead ached. Her grandmother laughed. “She can't see little eyebrows from there. Wave and call her name.” Himani stuck her arm out and shouted, “Sunaina! Skip with me later?” Sunaina looked up and waved the rope.

qa.q: What was Sunaina holding on her doorstep?
qa.a: A skipping rope.

qa.q: What might Himani have been feeling when she flashed her eyebrows bigger and bigger?
qa.a: She was probably excited and eager to be noticed, and a bit frustrated that the signal was not working. It is also possible she was just enjoying making funny faces through the window.

qa.q: What could Himani try the next time a friend is far away?
qa.a: She could wave and call the friend's name straight away, as her grandmother suggested, because a quick eyebrow flash is hard to see from a distance.

qa.q: Why might Sunaina not have reacted at first?
qa.a: She was busy skipping and was too far away to notice a small face signal through a bus window.

grounding: A child uses a brief eyebrow flash to greet and invite a game, it is missed, and a wave and spoken invitation work instead.

passage: On the stairs of their building in Osaka, Hana met Kwame from the fourth floor. She lifted her eyebrows quickly and smiled. Kwame flashed his brows right back. Hana's mother, carrying the groceries, said, “Oh, you two said hello with your faces! Can you say it with words too?” Hana giggled. “Hello, Kwame. Want to race to the landing?” “Hello! Yes!” said Kwame. They thumped up the steps, and at the top Hana flashed her eyebrows again, which now clearly meant, “Again?”

qa.q: Where did Hana meet Kwame?
qa.a: On the stairs of their building in Osaka.

qa.q: What was Hana feeling when she flashed her eyebrows at Kwame on the stairs?
qa.a: She was likely happy to see him and feeling playful, using the flash as a friendly hello. It could also have been a small surprise at bumping into him.

qa.q: How did Hana's mother help the greeting?
qa.a: She noticed the face hello and asked the children to say it in words too, which turned the signal into a clear invitation to play.

qa.q: How might Kwame understand Hana's last eyebrow flash at the top?
qa.a: After the race, he would likely read it as “Again?” because they now shared the game, so the same small signal carried a clearer meaning.

grounding: Two children exchange a quick eyebrow flash as hello, and adding spoken words makes the invitation to play clear.

passage:
The clinic waiting room was crowded and quiet. Varun, holding his father's hand, spotted a girl on the next bench with a toy car. He raised his eyebrows at her, quick, up and down, and grinned.

Sarika didn't notice. She was busy rolling the car along her mother's knee.

Varun tried again. Eyebrows up, down. Nothing.

His father leaned over. "Maybe say it with words too."

Varun slid off the bench. "Hi! Can I race your car?"

Sarika looked up and held it out.

qa.q: What was Sarika rolling the toy car along?
qa.a: Her mother's knee.

qa.q: What did Varun want when he flashed his eyebrows at Sarika?
qa.a: He was most likely feeling friendly and eager to play, using the eyebrow flash as a quick hello. Another reading is that he was just curious about the toy car.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying "Hi! Can I race your car?" worked because the quick eyebrow signal was easy to miss, and the words made his invitation clear.

qa.q: What is it like for Sarika when Varun first raises his eyebrows?
qa.a: She doesn't notice at all, because she is busy with her car, so to her nothing has happened yet.

grounding: It shows a child flashing his eyebrows as a quick hello and invitation, and a spoken greeting making it clear when the signal is missed.
